items.prompt_md: In a k-way merge with a heap, what does the heap hold at any moment?
options: Every item from every list, fully sorted
The `k` largest items seen so far
One candidate (the current front) from each sorted source that still has items
Only the final answer
items.answer: One candidate (the current front) from each sorted source that still has items
items.explanation_md: The heap is a frontier: the smallest unseen item overall is always the front of some source. Holding everything would defeat the point, and a top-k size-k heap is a different pattern.

items.prompt_md: After popping the smallest entry, what do you push?
options: The successor of the popped item within its own sorted source, if it has one
The largest item of every other source
The smallest item of the next source
Nothing; the heap only shrinks
items.answer: The successor of the popped item within its own sorted source, if it has one
items.explanation_md: The source that just lost its front must now offer its next element so the frontier again has one candidate per source. Without this, items would be skipped.

items.prompt_md: For the k-smallest-pair-sums task on sorted `nums1`, `nums2`, why is each row of sums `nums1[i] + nums2[j]` (varying `j`) sorted?
options: Because `nums2` is sorted, adding the same `nums1[i]` to larger values gives larger sums
Because the heap sorts it
Because `nums1` is sorted, so all sums are sorted globally
Rows are not sorted; only columns are
items.answer: Because `nums2` is sorted, adding the same `nums1[i]` to larger values gives larger sums
items.explanation_md: Fixing `i` adds a constant, so order follows `nums2`. By the same argument columns are sorted too, but the grid is not sorted globally, which is why a heap is needed to compare rows.

items.prompt_md: The frontier is seeded with the first pair of every row and each row advances only along its own columns. Why is no `seen` set required?
options: Each cell can be reached from only one predecessor (its left neighbour), so it is pushed at most once
Heaps automatically remove duplicates
The sums are all distinct for sorted input
Duplicates are harmless because the answer allows them
items.answer: Each cell can be reached from only one predecessor (its left neighbour), so it is pushed at most once
items.explanation_md: Seeding the whole first column and moving only right gives each cell a unique path. If you seeded only the top-left cell and pushed both right and down, a cell would be reachable two ways and need a `seen` set.

items.prompt_md: Let `m = min(k, len(nums1))` rows be seeded and `k` pairs be popped. What is the time of the heap solution?
options: O(n * m * log(n * m))
O(m + k log m)
O(k)
items.answer: O(m + k log m)
items.explanation_md: Heapify is O(m); then at most `k` pops and `k` pushes each cost O(log m) because the heap never has more than `m` entries. The first option is the brute force (build and sort everything).

items.prompt_md: What is the extra space (excluding the output list) of the heap solution for k smallest pair sums?
options: O(n * m), the grid is built
O(k) always, one entry per result
O(min(k, n)), one entry per seeded row
items.answer: O(min(k, n)), one entry per seeded row
items.explanation_md: The frontier never exceeds one entry per row, and only the first `min(k, n)` rows can contribute to the first `k` results. The grid is never stored.

items.prompt_md: You merge `K` sorted lists holding `N` items total into one sorted list using a heap with one entry per list. What is the time complexity?
options: O(N log K)
O(N * K)
O(K log N)
O(N log N)
items.answer: O(N log K)
items.explanation_md: Every one of the `N` items is popped and its successor pushed, each at O(log K) since the heap holds at most `K` entries. Concatenating and sorting would be O(N log N), which ignores the existing order.

items.prompt_md:
Given heap entries `(sum, i, j)`, what does this code do?

```python
_, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
out.append([a[i], b[j]])
if j + 1 < len(b):
    heapq.heappush(heap, (a[i] + b[j + 1], i, j + 1))
```
options: Outputs the smallest remaining pair and pushes the next pair from the same row
Outputs the largest pair and removes its row
Outputs a pair and pushes the next pair from the next row
Sorts `b` in place
items.answer: Outputs the smallest remaining pair and pushes the next pair from the same row
items.explanation_md: `i` is the row (index into `a`), `j` the column (index into `b`); incrementing `j` moves along the same sorted row. Moving to the next row would change `i`, which the code does not do.

items.prompt_md: Why is it enough to seed only `min(k, len(nums1))` rows instead of all of them?
options: Rows past the first `k` have strictly larger first sums, so they cannot appear in the first `k` results
The heap is limited to `k` entries by the language
Later rows are always duplicates of earlier ones
It is not enough; every row must be seeded
items.answer: Rows past the first `k` have strictly larger first sums, so they cannot appear in the first `k` results
items.explanation_md: With `nums1` sorted ascending, row `i` has at least `i` rows whose first sum is no larger (ties aside), so by row `k` those earlier rows already provide `k` candidates at least as small. Seeding all rows is still correct, just wasteful.

items.prompt_md: `k` is larger than `len(nums1) * len(nums2)`. What should a correct implementation return?
options: An error
All `len(nums1) * len(nums2)` pairs, in non-decreasing sum order
`k` pairs, repeating some
An empty list
items.answer: All `len(nums1) * len(nums2)` pairs, in non-decreasing sum order
items.explanation_md: The loop condition `heap and len(out) < k` stops when the heap empties, so every cell is output once. This is a classic edge case to mention.

items.prompt_md: Where would a k-way merge heap be a **poor** fit?
options: Merging 100 sorted log files by timestamp
Finding the k smallest items across several sorted lists
Finding the k largest items of one unsorted array
Merging sorted rows of a matrix
items.answer: Finding the k largest items of one unsorted array
items.explanation_md: There are no sorted sources to merge; the right tool is a size-k heap over a scan (Top-K) or quickselect. The other three have sorted sources with a natural successor.

items.prompt_md: A search service has 50 shards, each returning its results already sorted by score. You must return the 20 best-scoring results across all shards. Which technique fits?
options: Concatenate all shard results and sort
A min-heap holding the current front of each shard, popped 20 times
Binary search on the score
A trie of result titles
items.answer: A min-heap holding the current front of each shard, popped 20 times
items.explanation_md: Each shard is a sorted source, so a frontier heap with one candidate per shard yields the next best result each time. Concatenating and sorting ignores the existing order and costs far more than needed.

items.prompt_md: Each row and each column of an `n` by `n` grid is sorted ascending. You need the k-th smallest value without building a flat sorted copy. Which technique fits?
options: A frontier min-heap seeded with row heads, advancing right after each pop
Prefix sums over the grid
A monotonic stack per column
Union-find over the cells
items.answer: A frontier min-heap seeded with row heads, advancing right after each pop
items.explanation_md: Each row is a sorted list, so this is a k-way merge stopped after `k` pops. The other structures answer connectivity, ranges or next-greater queries, not ordered extraction.

items.prompt_md: You must generate the first `n` numbers whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5, in increasing order. Which technique fits?
options: Binary search on the value
Merge three sorted streams (multiples by 2, 3 and 5) with a heap or three pointers
Backtracking over factor combinations
A sliding window over integers
items.answer: Merge three sorted streams (multiples by 2, 3 and 5) with a heap or three pointers
items.explanation_md: Each new number is an earlier number times 2, 3 or 5, and each of those multiplier sequences is increasing: three sorted sources merged on the fly. Backtracking would enumerate far too many values out of order.

items.prompt_md: You have `k` sorted lists of integers and must find the narrowest numeric range that includes at least one value from every list. Which technique fits?
options: Sort each list descending and zip them
A hash map of values to list ids
Keep a min-heap of the current front of each list while tracking the current maximum, advancing the smallest
Dynamic programming on list pairs
items.answer: Keep a min-heap of the current front of each list while tracking the current maximum, advancing the smallest
items.explanation_md: The frontier (one element per list) always spans a candidate range from the heap minimum to the tracked maximum; advancing the minimum is the only way to tighten it. That is the k-way merge frontier with extra bookkeeping.

items.prompt_md: Two sorted linked lists must be merged into one sorted linked list in O(n) time and O(1) extra pointers. Which technique fits?
options: A min-heap of all nodes
Two-pointer splice using a dummy head node
Binary search for each node's position
Quickselect
items.answer: Two-pointer splice using a dummy head node
items.explanation_md: With only two sources a single comparison picks the next node, so a heap adds overhead for nothing. The heap pays off once there are many lists.

items.prompt_md: Given an unsorted array and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent values. Which technique fits?
options: Count with a hash map, then keep a size-`k` heap (or bucket sort) over the counts
A frontier heap merging sorted rows
Binary search on the frequency
A sliding window of size `k`
items.answer: Count with a hash map, then keep a size-`k` heap (or bucket sort) over the counts
items.explanation_md: There are no sorted sources to merge; it is a counting job followed by a Top-K selection. A frontier heap needs sorted rows with successors.

items.prompt_md: A sorted array of positive integers is given, and you need to know whether any two elements add to a target. Which technique fits?
options: A min-heap seeded with all pair sums
Two pointers moving inward from both ends
A k-way merge of sorted rows
Recursion with memoisation
items.answer: Two pointers moving inward from both ends
items.explanation_md: A yes/no pair query on sorted data is solved by squeezing inward in O(n). Enumerating pair sums, even lazily with a heap, is more machinery than the question needs.

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted matrix whose rows and columns increase, determine whether a specific value is present. Which technique fits?
options: A k-way merge heap over every row
Staircase search from a corner, discarding a row or column per step
A segment tree
Building a trie of digits
items.answer: Staircase search from a corner, discarding a row or column per step
items.explanation_md: Membership in a doubly sorted grid is answered in O(rows + cols) by walking from a corner; no ordered extraction of many items is needed, so the merge heap would be overkill.

items.prompt_md: A scheduler must always run the pending job with the earliest deadline next, and new jobs keep arriving. Which technique fits?
options: Backtracking
A priority queue keyed on deadline
A fixed-size sliding window
A prefix-sum array
items.answer: A priority queue keyed on deadline
items.explanation_md: Dynamic arrivals plus repeated extract-min is the plain heap use. There are no pre-sorted sources, so it is not a merge, but the structure is the same priority queue.

items.prompt_md: A telemetry system has 200 time-ordered event streams and wants a single merged stream in chronological order, consumed lazily one event at a time. Which technique fits?
options: Load every event into memory and sort
Union-find to group streams
A heap holding the next event from each stream, popping and refilling from that stream
A stack of pending events
items.answer: A heap holding the next event from each stream, popping and refilling from that stream
items.explanation_md: The merge needs only one buffered event per stream, so memory is O(streams) and each event costs O(log streams). Loading everything breaks laziness and memory limits.
